title: Interop playbook pilot — SDK + OpenAI-compat endpoints (Argus Payments)
header:
Date: 2026-09-08 | Time: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Banerjee (Redwood SA); Renee Park, Tom Alvarez, Meena Patel, Chris Osei (Argus Payments)
summary: POC scoping call to define pilot success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plan, timeline and integration approach. Focus on OpenAI-compatible endpoints, SDK usage, function/tool calling for payment orchestration, and structured JSON outputs for downstream systems. Security and PCI-adjacent controls (VPC, KMS, audit logs) are key blockers for Argus. Agreed next step: Redwood to deliver SOW + benchmark plan and provide sample scripts for latency/throughput tests against a dedicated pilot environment.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um yeah quick intros. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Diego is our SE, Aisha is solutions.
[00:08] Renee Park: Renee here, thanks, we'll go through what we need for a pilot. Busy week so appreciate the time.
[00:13] Diego Ruiz: Cool. Quick agenda — define success, understand your workload, scope benchmarks, and align on timeline.
[00:21] Tom Alvarez: Right. At Argus Payments we want to evaluate embedding a fraud-assist + payment orchestration assistant. The, uh, constraints are: PCI-adjacent data never leaves our VPC, we need audit trails, and 250ms p95 is ideal for short inference calls.
[00:37] Aisha Banerjee: Quick clarifying q — when you say 250ms p95, is that for generation of <64 token responses for routing decisions?
[00:44] Tom Alvarez: Exactly. Most calls are short: prompt+few tokens, but we also have batched reconciliation jobs that can be longer.
[00:51] Diego Ruiz: OK. For the short path we can prioritize hosted vs dedicated. Hosted will give fastest onboarding but VPC/private needs either Redwood Dedicated or Private with VPC peering. We'll list both options in the pilot SOW.
[01:02] Meena Patel: Security is non-negotiable. We need SAML SSO, RBAC, KMS/HSM for key wrap, and audit logs exported to our SIEM. Also SOC2 + penetration test report.
[01:14] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll attach the security pack — SAML, SSO, audit log retention, and our SOC2 report. For KMS we support customer-managed keys and HSM integration on Private.
[01:23] Chris Osei: From product POV we need structured JSON outputs for the orchestration layer. Example: {decision: approve/decline, reason_code: string, risk_score: float, actions:[...]} — can Redwood validate schema server-side?
[01:36] Diego Ruiz: Yes; we have structured output support and schema enforcement on the API with failure modes (reject / best-effort). For the POC we'll demo strict schema validation and a relaxed mode. There may be a small latency delta when strict validation + type coercion is enabled.
[01:48] Tom Alvarez: How do function calls look? We need the model to call internal microservices (e.g., look up customer history) but we can't expose that publicly.
[01:55] Aisha Banerjee: Our OpenAI-compatible function-calling layer supports tool invocation patterns; for Private/Dedicated we'll run the function proxy in your VPC so secrets never leave. For hosted we have a secure connector but that may not meet your PCI-adjacent constraints.
[02:07] Renee Park: So pilot options: 1) short hosted trial with sanitized data; 2) dedicated pilot cluster reserved for you; 3) private deployment in your cloud.
[02:17] Tom Alvarez: Yes, we'd like to see a dedicated pilot cluster first, maybe escalate to Private if numbers look good.
[02:21] Diego Ruiz: Good. For sizing, can you share typical QPS and token distribution?
[02:27] Chris Osei: We ran a trace — 150 TPS at peak across our auth path, but 80% are sub-second simple prompts, average prompt length 40 tokens, response 20 tokens. Monthly active calls ~1.2M.
[02:39] Maya Chen: Nice detail. For initial pilot we'll do a traffic replay of a subset — say 100k requests over 48 hours — to capture tail latency. We'll need a sample trace and a small dataset of de-identified prompts.
[02:51] Tom Alvarez: We can provide that by Friday. Security will sanitize PII.
[02:55] Meena Patel: We'll need to review pilot network topology and ensure peering is possible. Also log retention and where logs land.
[03:03] Diego Ruiz: We'll provide a network topology doc. On benchmarking, plan is: latency microbenchmarks (p95/p99), throughput ramps to find sustainable QPS, and a cost-per-1M tokens estimate under expected batching.
[03:17] Chris Osei: About batching — our main concern is latency. We prefer smaller batch sizes but we also need cost predictability.
[03:23] Diego Ruiz: Right — Redwood Optimize will recommend batch/config. For the pilot we'll test two configs: latency-optimized (small batch, pre-warmed cache) and cost-optimized (larger batch, more KV cache reuse). We'll capture token-per-dollar metrics.
[03:36] Tom Alvarez: How do we instrument the results in our side? We need traces and per-token cost breakdown.
[03:41] Aisha Banerjee: The Redwood Console can export per-route dashboards and token-level cost. We'll provide a temporary read-only dashboard and a CSV export for your finance team.
[03:50] Renee Park: Timeline — what's realistic for a 6-week pilot?
[03:53] Maya Chen: Proposed: Week 0 — SOW + environment setup; Week 1 — data sanitization + credential exchange; Week 2 — baseline benchmarks; Week 3 — integration and schema tests; Week 4 — traffic replay and ramp; Week 5 — tuning and cost analysis; Week 6 — final report and go/no-go.
[04:12] Tom Alvarez: That looks good. Stakeholders: we need Product, Platform, Security, and a finance readout at the end.
[04:19] Meena Patel: Also legal will want contract language around data retention and indemnity.
[04:23] Maya Chen: We'll include sample contract clauses and a pilot SOW with cancellation terms.
[04:27] Chris Osei: For tool calling, we need example flows: 1) model decides to check account risk -> function call to accounts service -> response -> structured decision. Can the Redwood SDK do this end-to-end?
[04:38] Diego Ruiz: Yes. We'll provide SDK samples in Node and Python showing OpenAI-compatible endpoints and local proxying for function calls. We'll include a sample orchestration repo.
[04:47] Tom Alvarez: Any limits on KV cache size or model variants? We plan to test a few models including Llama-like 13B quantized and a higher-capability 70B variant for complex reasoning.
[04:58] Aisha Banerjee: The runtime supports a range of quantized models; we'll include recommended kernel/quantization settings per model. KV cache sizing is configurable; we'll outline memory footprints per variant in the SOW. For the pilot we'll recommend starting with a 13B int8 for latency tests and 70B for regression validation.
[05:13] Meena Patel: Audit trail question — can we ship audit logs to our Splunk via S3 or streaming?
[05:18] Diego Ruiz: Yes, logs can be exported to S3 with lifecycle and you can have a connector to Splunk. For Private we can push logs directly to your collector.
[05:25] Renee Park: What about failover — if primary model is overloaded, can we fallback to a smaller model automatically?
[05:31] Diego Ruiz: Absolutely. We'll set routing policies — primary latency tier, fallback to cheaper model. Canary rollouts also supported.
[05:37] Tom Alvarez: Ok great. What are the acceptance criteria?
[05:39] Maya Chen: Proposed success criteria for the pilot:
- Latency: p95 < 300ms for short path (note: we conservatively set 300ms vs 250ms target)
- Functionality: structured-output validation success rate > 98% in strict mode
- Reliability: availability >= 99.5% during benchmark window
- Cost: projected token cost within agreed budget threshold (to be defined in SOW)
- Security: pass initial security checklist (SAML, KMS, audit logs)
[06:05] Tom Alvarez: That looks reasonable. We'll aim to move the 250ms internal target to 300ms for the pilot.
[06:09] Meena Patel: Legal and Security need the draft SOW and network diagram by Monday.
[06:14] Maya Chen: We'll get you a draft SOW, security pack, network diagram, and benchmark plan by Monday COB.
[06:20] Chris Osei: For the demos, can you show structured-output failure handling? We want to see when model returns malformed JSON.
[06:26] Diego Ruiz: Yep, demo will include strict validation rejection path and auto-repair suggestions in relaxed mode.
[06:32] Tom Alvarez: Any blockers on our side? We need to confirm cloud account permissions for peering and give a service account for the traffic replay.
[06:40] Renee Park: I'll follow up with infra to get those permissions.
[06:44] Maya Chen: Great. We'll also attach sample benchmark scripts and a shim you can run to anonymize traces.
[06:51] Meena Patel: Also want to check data residency — we'll likely require EU region for some test data.
[06:56] Aisha Banerjee: Noted — we can run pilot shards in eu-west and us-west as needed.
[07:01] Chris Osei: Ok let's recap next steps.
[07:03] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to send SOW, security pack, network diagram, benchmark scripts, and SDK samples by Monday. Argus to provide sanitized trace, service account, and confirm stakeholders. Schedule: kickoff next Tuesday to start week 0.
[07:15] Tom Alvarez: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[07:18] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the calendar invite and SOW.
[07:22] [call ends]

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hears — some technical terms transcribed loosely (e.g., KV cache heard as "KV case"). There was light crosstalk between Diego and Aisha on the function proxy sequencing.
next_steps: Redwood to deliver pilot SOW, security pack, network topology and benchmark plan by 2026-09-11 (Maya)
Argus to provide de-identified trace and service account details by 2026-09-11 (Renee/Tom)
Schedule pilot kickoff session for 2026-09-15 to begin Week 0 setup (all)
